summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of how people protect the ocean: marine protected areas (MPAs) as refuges where populations recover and 'spill over' to nearby fished waters; sustainable fishing as harvesting at or below a stock's replacement rate so it persists; and actions across scales (personal plastic reduction, local/national reserves and catch limits, international emissions agreements). The empirical core (yield vs replacement, MPA recovery/spillover) is quantitative and modelable; a genuine values trade-off (fishing livelihoods vs conservation) should be surfaced as decision-making, not a good-vs-bad story. Pair each protective action with the specific problem it targets.
misconceptions: 'Sustainable fishing means stop fishing' — rather than harvesting within the stock's replacement rate.
'An MPA just fences off fish uselessly' — missing recovery and spillover that benefit surrounding waters too.
'One person recycling can't matter / only governments can act' — or the opposite, that personal acts alone are enough; missing the range of scales.
'Protecting the ocean has no costs or trade-offs' — ignoring livelihoods, enforcement and competing interests.
Thinking a depleted stock instantly refills once fishing stops — underestimating recovery time and thresholds.

activities.title: Manage the fishery: catch vs replacement and the reserve effect
steps: Take charge of a struggling fishery with two controls: how much to catch each year, and how large a no-fishing marine protected area to set aside.
First try a high catch and track the fish population and the fishers' income over several seasons; record what happens when catch exceeds what the stock can replace.
Lower the annual catch to around the rate the stock replenishes and observe whether the population stabilises.
Set aside an MPA and watch across seasons whether the protected core rebuilds and whether young fish 'spill over' the boundary to raise catches nearby.
Write down, for each setting you tried, what happened to BOTH fish population and income, and state the catch/reserve combination that lasts.
activities.insight: A fish stock replenishes itself, so in this model, harvesting at or below its replacement rate can continue season after season, while over-harvesting that goes on shrinks the stock and can collapse it. How fast a stock replaces itself depends on how many fish are left, so a depleted stock refills slowly. A protected refuge lets fish grow and breed and, through spillover, can pay back the fishery it seems to close. Protection is not 'stop fishing everywhere' but fishing within what the ocean can renew.

activities.title: Negotiate a catch limit or reserve: whose needs?
steps: Take a role in a negotiation to set a catch limit or site a reserve, speaking in turn as a fisher who needs income and a marine scientist who needs the stock to recover.
State each side's interest in your own words, then propose a catch limit or reserve boundary and justify it against both recovery and livelihoods.
Explain one cost of your chosen measure (lost fishing ground, enforcement, short-term income) and how it might pay back over time.
activities.insight: Protecting the ocean involves competing interests and real costs; good decisions weigh recovery against human needs rather than treating conservation as cost-free.

activities.title: Match each ocean problem to its protective action
steps: Match each threat to a remedy that actually targets it: plastic litter → beach clean-ups and reducing plastic use; overfishing → reserves and catch limits; ocean acidification → cutting carbon emissions.
Explore a diagram of an MPA labelled with a protected core, a spillover zone, and a surrounding fished zone, and describe in your own words how the core helps the fished zone.
Place protective actions on a scales-of-action ladder: personal (reduce plastic) → local/national (reserves, catch limits) → international (emissions agreements).
Explain why cutting carbon emissions counts as ocean protection even though it is about the air (CO2 drives acidification), and name one ocean problem beach clean-ups do NOT fix.
activities.insight: Different threats need different, matched remedies acting at different scales; no single action fixes everything, and both personal and collective/policy levers matter.

activities.title: Check and defend the reasoning (diagnostic)
steps: Respond to this scenario: A town wants more fish for years to come, so a scientist suggests making part of the bay a marine protected area where NO fishing is allowed at all. A child objects: 'that's silly — if you stop fishing there you'll get FEWER fish to catch, not more.' Do you agree, and how could closing an area to fishing end up giving people MORE fish?
Explain how leaving big fish alone in a reserve could put MORE fish in the nets of boats fishing just outside it.
Define 'sustainable' precisely: what exactly has to be true about how much we take for fishing to go on forever?
Define what an MPA is and name at least two actions people can take to protect oceans.
activities.insight: A learner who sees fish as a fixed stock to divide thinks any closed area means fewer fish; a learner who understands replenishment sees that protection lets breeding recover and spill over, which can raise nearby catches over time, especially where the stock had been overfished.

checkQuestion: A town wants more fish for years to come, so a scientist suggests making part of the bay a marine protected area where NO fishing is allowed at all. A child objects: 'that's silly — if you stop fishing there you'll get FEWER fish to catch, not more'. Do you agree — and how could closing an area to fishing end up giving people MORE fish?
checkAnswer: The child's objection is wrong. A marine protected area lets fish live, grow big and breed undisturbed; those larger fish produce far more young, and fish (and their eggs and larvae) spill over into the surrounding waters where people CAN fish. So protecting one area can raise catches nearby over time. This works together with sustainable fishing — taking only what the ocean can replace — so the population keeps refilling itself instead of being emptied.
